entries.subject: Ó Fionnagáin et al. (2022) magnetohydrodynamic simulations of ε Eridani, Zenodo 5575241: gas density for the magnetic maps of January 2008, October 2011 and October 2013
entries.finding: The deposit is one tar.gz of 6,355,199,342 bytes (CC BY 4.0) holding nine BATS-R-US solution files in Tecplot binary version 112, each one zone of bricks with about 10 million nodes on a block-adaptive grid of ±50 stellar radii, with position, density, velocity, magnetic field, wave energies, pressures and currents. Three magnetic maps, each with three runs ten minutes after an eruption near the equator (+10°) or either pole (±70°). Resampled onto a 128³ cube of ±4 radii, every voxel outside the star is covered. At 2 radii the densest twentieth of directions is 10, 9 and 15 times the thinnest, for the three maps in order.

entries.subject: Which of a map's three eruption runs is drawn
entries.finding: The steady state the eruptions start from is not in the deposit. A run is taken as disturbed where its density is more than 1.25 times from the median of the three runs of its map. That share of the drawn volume (1 to 4 radii) is, for the equator, north and south runs: 5.6%, 7.1%, 11.5% (January 2008); 9.4%, 10.4%, 14.8% (October 2011); 3.7%, 4.4%, 6.4% (October 2013). The equator run is the least disturbed every time and is the one drawn. The disturbed voxels lie at mean latitude -1°, +10° and +19° in the equator runs, +42° to +56° in the north runs and -41° to -45° in the south runs, which matches the file names; the October 2013 equator file carries no site in its name. Two runs depart at once in 0.6% to 1.3% of the volume.

entries.subject: Drawing the median of the three runs as the steady corona
entries.finding: The median of a map's three runs is the steady state wherever at most one eruption reaches, which is all but about 1% of the drawn volume. It is a statistic over three released instants, not a state the authors released, so it is used only to measure each eruption and not drawn. The authors offer the full set, with the steady states, on request.

entries.subject: How the simulation's axes are placed on the sky
entries.finding: The rotation axis is drawn 46° from the line of sight, the inclination Jeffers et al. (2017) fit (46 ± 2°); Petit et al. (2021) use the same. These papers give no position angle of the axis on the sky, and the rotation phase today would need the 11.7-day rotation tracked from the map dates, which they do not give. The axis is drawn tilted toward north and the map's zero longitude toward Earth, stated as conventions.

entries.subject: How density becomes brightness
entries.finding: On the logarithmic density scale the Sun's STEREO dataset uses, the simulation's tenfold contrast between directions becomes a quarter of the scale and the summed line of sight looks almost as smooth as a spherical model. Shown through a radial filter, with brightness proportional to density at each distance and 10 times the typical density fully bright, the dense sheets and thin regions show at every distance. The typical density of a radius is the median over the sphere, averaged in the logarithm over the three drawn runs: 3.6e8 electrons per cm³ at 1.1 radii, 1.2e7 at 2, 2.2e6 at 3, 8.9e5 at 3.9.

entries.subject: Parker's isothermal wind with the mass loss of Wood et al. (2002) and the X-ray temperature of Bennedik et al. (2026)
entries.finding: Mass loss 30 times the Sun's (2e-14 solar masses a year) and 4.06 million kelvin give 6.2e7 electrons per cm³ at the surface, 5.8e6 at 2 radii and 8.9e5 at 4, leaving at 93 km/s and passing the speed of sound at 1.89 radii. Against the simulation's typical density it is 0.12 times at 1.1 radii, 0.50 at 2, 0.86 at 3 and 1.07 at 3.9: within 15% beyond 3 radii, too thin close to the star, where the magnetic field holds the gas. With the Sun's numbers at solar minimum (Johnstone & Güdel 2015, Table 1) the same model is 20 times the density STEREO COR1-B measured at 1.5 solar radii and 0.65 times at 4; with the temperature at maximum, 0.13 to 0.48 times.

entries.subject: Gas at rest at one temperature, its amount from the X-ray luminosity
entries.finding: With log L_X 28.35 and 0.35 keV (Bennedik et al. 2026, Table 5) and the radiative loss of Rosner, Tucker & Vaiana (1978), the base density is 6.5e8 electrons per cm³ and the scale height 0.26 radii. It is 1.3 times the simulation's typical density at 1.1 radii, 8 times at 2 and 44 times at 3.9, and 43 times the measured wind at 4 radii. The temperature the law of Bennedik et al. gives for the star's X-ray surface flux, 3.95 million kelvin, changes the picture by 3%. With the Sun's numbers at solar minimum it is 0.31 times the density STEREO measured at 1.5 solar radii and 0.01 times at 4. Left out.

entries.subject: Other published simulations and magnetic maps of this star
entries.finding: Alvarado-Gómez et al. (2016, A&A 588, A28 and 594, A95) simulated this star's corona and wind from the January 2010 map but deposited no data; they print a mean density of 3.4e7 and 8.3e7 electrons per cm³ between 1.05 and 1.5 radii for their two map versions. No deposit of the magnetic maps of Jeffers et al. (2014, 2017) or Petit et al. (2021) was found at CDS or Zenodo. Two Zenodo searches on 2026-10-05, 198 dataset records by topic and 39 star names against wind, corona and magnetic-map terms, found no other star's corona simulation with data files.

entries.subject: The simulation's magnetic field as a dataset of its own
entries.finding: The files carry the field vector. Its strength, resampled with the density, has a median of 6.8, 5.8 and 14.0 gauss at 1.1 radii for the three maps and falls to about 1 gauss at 3.9 radii. It is read but not drawn: field lines would say more than a strength volume, and no shared owner draws lines yet.
